source.title: Unveiling Memorization-Generalization Coexistence: A Case Study on Arithmetic Tasks with Label Noise

record.tranche_reason: The study varies network width and measures test performance under label noise, directly testing model-wise double descent with the same size-sweep and test-error behavior, in a new arithmetic-task setting.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly reports model-wise double descent and a regularization-dependent shift in its threshold. Epoch-wise test-accuracy curves report delayed generalization (grokking), not an explicit fall-rise-fall test-error pattern. Training-ratio curves are shown, but no textual result says that more data raises test error near interpolation. Values available only as plotted curves are recorded as figure-only.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps hidden width in two-layer networks trained on modular arithmetic with injected label noise. It reports clean test error (1 − accuracy) against width, and states that model-wise double descent is observed across activations, optimizers, training ratios and tasks. This is the original width-sweep and test-error method, applied in a new task setting. The width–error result is a secondary finding; the paper's main focus is memorization–generalization mechanisms.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaced in emphasis. The main conclusion is that over-parameterized networks internally learn the arithmetic rule even under heavy label noise (up to ~80%), but this rule is masked by noise memorization. Frequency filtration can recover it, while task-agnostic neuron selection gives only limited gains because generalization is spread across neurons. Model-wise double descent (bigger models generalize better once properly regularized; weight decay shifts the threshold; misspecification breaks this) is a supporting finding from Section 3.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a model-width sweep and test-performance measurement comparable to the original empirical method, but studies two-layer networks on modular arithmetic tasks with explicit label noise and varied optimizers, activations, and weight decay.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported threshold and second-descent regime depend on weight decay; activation functions have different test-accuracy ceilings; architecture expressivity and noise symmetry affect whether the model can interpolate noisy labels.
record.problems: Most width-dependent results are presented as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The experiments use controlled arithmetic tasks and two-layer networks; the authors note that model misspecification can prevent interpolation.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-width curves for additional optimizer, activation, arithmetic-task, and noise-ratio combinations are not separately transcribed; the paper summarizes them as consistent model-wise double descent in Section 3.1 and Appendix C.1 (Figures 1, 8, and 11–13). Detailed epoch-curve combinations are likewise not transcribed separately (Appendix C.4, Figures 16–21).

untested.parts: Whether test error over epochs follows fall-rise-fall. Only grokking curves are reported.
Whether more training samples raise test error near the threshold. Training ratios 40/50/60% appear only as separate width-sweep figures, with no stated comparison.
Non-neural model classes; only two-layer networks are tested.
EMC is invoked as an explanation for the weight-decay shift, but no complexity measure is computed or used to predict the peak.
Whether the peak scales with label noise, whether multiple peaks occur, and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
No re-expression of complexity as an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Tied model under asymmetric noise with stronger weight decay: regularization mitigates misspecification and recovers good generalization. This bears on regularization dependence (V6) and on the V1 limitation.
Test cross-entropy is lower (more confident) in the over-parameterized regime than in the under-parameterized regime. This is a second-descent result on the loss measure.
Across-ratio comparison of test accuracy at fixed width (40/50/60% training ratio), readable only from figures. A researcher would need it to check V3.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T1 because the width sweep and test-error measure match the original method; the setting is novel (modular arithmetic with label noise), so T3 would also be defensible. The paper cites Nakkiran et al. for EMC but does not test it. No numerical values or uncertainty are given for any double-descent curve; all evidence is plotted curves plus textual summary. Other findings (noisy labels memorized faster early in training; frequency filtration; neuron partitioning) are outside the double-descent versions.

versions.untested_parts: The claim's universality beyond the tested two-layer networks, arithmetic tasks, and reported configurations.
The paper reports test-accuracy training curves and delayed generalization, but does not establish whether test error follows a fall-rise-fall curve over epochs.
Training ratios are varied and curves are shown, but the text does not report whether increasing sample count raises test error near interpolation; figure-only rows do not determine the direction.
The study tests multiple neural-network activation functions and arithmetic tasks, not a broad range of non-neural model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The study varies label-noise ratios and regularization, but does not test whether noise causes the peak, whether multiple peaks arise, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.stage_stated: trained for 200,000 epochs unless stated otherwise
rows.operation_detail: Swept hidden-layer width and measured clean test performance on noisy modular-arithmetic tasks.

conditions.value: varied; includes ReLU, quadratic, GeLU, and LeakyReLU
AdamW, Adam, and Muon; other settings also reported

rows.measure: Test error (1 − test accuracy) versus model width
rows.value: The paper reports non-monotonic test error that worsens near the interpolation threshold and improves again as model size increases; within the over-parameterized regime, test accuracy is non-decreasing with size.
rows.note: The reported finding summarizes results across varying setups; individual curve values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: Remove V4: only two-layer neural networks are tested, so there are no non-neural model classes. Remove V6: this row does not isolate noise or regularization effects.

rows.subject: ReLU two-layer neural network
rows.size_stated: M varied; Figure 2 plots widths from 10¹ to 10⁴
rows.operation_detail: Compared width-dependent training and test performance at different weight-decay strengths.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and test cross-entropy versus model width; location of interpolation threshold
rows.value: Increasing weight decay shifts the interpolation threshold to larger sizes and delays the second-descent regime.
rows.note: The text describes the threshold shift but gives no numerical threshold locations.
rows.check: For V6 this row shows only that weight decay moves the threshold and delays the second descent. It does not test whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.

rows.subject: two-layer neural networks with quadratic or GeLU activation
rows.operation_detail: Compared test accuracy across increasing model widths.
rows.value: The paper reports clear ceilings in test accuracy within the explored model-size range.
rows.note: The reported ceilings qualify the claim of continuing improvement with greater size; the text does not say that these activations lack an initial double-descent pattern.
rows.check: Remove V4. The ceilings are saturation within the second descent; the text says accuracy is still non-decreasing and that double descent is seen across activations. Partial overstates the deviation.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, paragraph on quadratic and GeLU accuracy ceilings; Figure 1b.

rows.subject: first-layer-tied two-layer neural network (U = V)
rows.size_stated: model width varied; exact values not stated in the text
rows.operation_detail: Swept width for a tied architecture under asymmetric random label noise.
rows.measure: Training-label interpolation and test accuracy versus model width
rows.value: The tied model cannot interpolate all asymmetric noisy labels; the paper reports irregular test-accuracy curves and says test accuracy does not vary monotonically with width in this case.
rows.locator: Section 3.1 and Appendix C.2; Figure 15, left and right panels
rows.note: This is explicitly described as model misspecification: the over-parameterized interpolation regime does not strictly exist.
rows.check: Remove V4. With asymmetric noise the tied model cannot interpolate, so no clean interpolation peak or second descent appears. The condition also lists wd=5.0, whose result (Fig 15 right, regularization restores generalization) is not in the value.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V1: asymmetric noise prevents full interpolation, so the claimed interpolation transition is unavailable. Figure 15 left reports irregular accuracy at weight decay 0.1; the right panel reports improved generalization through noise suppression at weight decay 5.0.
